action: Mining operators using Luxor Commander: confirm your pool and payout settings match what you set, and review account access. Luxor says no customer action is needed.
exec: A single fleet-management dashboard let an intruder redirect miners' rewards, showing centralised control tools are a single point of failure.
impact: Hashrate from just over a dozen client accounts was sent to the OCEAN pool for up to about two hours; about 0.162 BTC reached the attacker's address, per The Cyber Express. Luxor says no data was taken and clients will be compensated.
plain: Hackers got into software that bitcoin miners use to manage their machines and pointed the machines at another mining pool, so the rewards went to the attacker. Luxor fixed it within two hours and says it will repay customers.
summary: Luxor Technology confirmed that from about 6 pm Pacific on 14 November an intruder used its Commander fleet-management platform to redirect hashrate from just over a dozen client accounts to the OCEAN pool. Luxor says it patched the flaw within two hours, restored settings, found no data exfiltrated, and will compensate clients and publish a post-mortem. Its CEO blamed an AI-enabled attack; the method is undisclosed.
title: Luxor Commander mining software hijacked to redirect clients' bitcoin hashrate

validation.note: The Cyber Express and CryptoSlate both report Luxor's own statements. The 64,000-machine and 13 EH/s scale is a third-party estimate (GalaxyMind) that Luxor has not confirmed; Luxor says just over a dozen accounts. The attack method and the AI-enabled claim come from Luxor's CEO and are unverified.

review.note: Compared with Cyber Express and CryptoSlate: 6pm PT 14 Nov, over a dozen accounts, patched in 2h, no exfiltration, CEO AI claim and scale estimate caveated
